summary: A white paper summarizing factors in judging whether an IPng proposal could succeed in the marketplace. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A paper about whether people will actually buy and use a new Internet design.

subtitle: Assessing whether IPng can win in the market against IPv4

tldr.problem: IPv4 is entrenched with a massive installed base. For IPng to be adopted, it must either offer compelling new capabilities, reduce costs, or provide access to IPng-only resources. But none of these incentives look strong, raising questions about market viability.
tldr.mechanism: This white paper analyzes the adoption barriers. It considers how technology can be pushed through bundling with operating systems, compares IPng against mature IPv4, and explores three paths for migration: new functionality, cost savings, and connectivity to otherwise unreachable hosts.
tldr.outcome: The paper concludes that without clearly improved functionality over IPv4 and transparent access between IPv4 and IPng communities, IPng adoption faces serious obstacles. Network address translation is likely to delay or complicate IPng deployment.

today: IPv6 was eventually standardized and deployed despite these market viability concerns. NAT has indeed become ubiquitous, extending IPv4's life far longer than predicted in 1994. However, IPv6 adoption has grown, driven by mobile devices, IoT, and the genuine exhaustion of IPv4 addresses by 2011. The RFC's skepticism turned out to be prescient about the challenges, though IPv6 succeeded anyway through a combination of standards mandate and technological necessity.

sections.title: The Challenge: IPv4 is Hard to Replace
sections.content:
This RFC was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550, examining market viability as a criterion for IPng selection. The core insight is blunt: in an open marketplace, customers adopt new technologies only if they offer clear benefits. Deploying new networking technology is difficult and expensive, so customers demand a compelling return on investment.

IPng must compete against IPv4, which is mature, stable, widely deployed, and thoroughly understood. Even if IPng is technically superior, switching requires tremendous effort and cost.
sections.plainLanguage: People will not switch to a new Internet unless they have a really good reason. Just being newer is not enough.

sections.title: Paths to IPng Migration
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three possible reasons existing IPv4 users might migrate to IPng:

New functionality: IPng must offer capabilities not found in IPv4, such as resource reservation, mobility, autoconfiguration, or security. However, there is uncertainty whether these will be in the base specification of any IPng candidate. Without tangible new features, there is no motivation to migrate.

Cost savings: Migration to IPng will almost certainly increase costs, not reduce them. Users must invest in training, engineering, and equipment. This path seems unlikely to drive adoption.

Connectivity to unreachable hosts: Existing sites with valid IPv4 addresses have no motivation to switch until address space is depleted. Only when IPv4 addresses run out and organizations exist that can only be reached via IPng will connectivity become a driver.
sections.plainLanguage: People might switch if IPng does something new, or if they have to. Just getting new addresses will not convince them.

sections.title: The NAT Problem and Market Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC raises a critical concern: when IPv4 addresses are exhausted, there will not be enough space to map all IPng addresses into IPv4 space. As none of the IPng proposals call for dynamic network address translation (NAT) at the time of writing, IPng-only sites will have access only to a partial set of IPv4 sites—clearly less valuable than complete Internet access.

Vendors will be motivated to develop NAT devices to bridge this gap, allowing "privately numbered" IPv4 networks to access the Internet transparently. This workaround could delay IPv6 deployment by extending the viability of IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: A trick called NAT might let people keep using old IPv4 for longer than expected, which slows down switching to IPng.

sections.title: The Viability Verdict
sections.content: The paper concludes that no vendor can afford to deploy products that the marketplace does not want. IPng cannot succeed without actual deployment by organizations. As currently envisioned, IPng may not be ambitious enough to compete against IPv4 and the inevitable arrival of NAT devices. To meet market viability requirements, IPng must deliver clearly improved functionality over IPv4 while offering transparent access between IPv4 and IPng communities once address depletion occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: For IPng to win, it has to be so much better that people want to switch, even though switching is hard and expensive.

references.text: RFC 1550 is referenced as the call for criteria.
